subject: Computer Networking
title: TCP: Reliable Transport
description: A micro-lesson that makes TCP: Reliable Transport usable.

hook.text: You download a file and expect every byte to arrive perfectly. TCP makes that promise.

buildup.text: TCP numbers each segment, tracks acknowledgments, and retransmits anything that goes missing.

discovery.text: It also controls flow — slowing down when the receiver is overwhelmed and speeding up when it's clear.

twist.text: All that bookkeeping adds latency. TCP prioritizes correctness over speed, every single time.

climax.text: Websites, email, file downloads — almost everything that must be correct uses TCP.

punchline.text: TCP delivers every byte, in order, no matter what.

details.summary: TCP provides reliable, ordered, error-checked delivery of data between applications over IP networks. It establishes connections with a three-way handshake, tracks every byte with sequence numbers, retransmits lost packets, and uses flow control to prevent overwhelming receivers.
details.whyItMatters: TCP carries the vast majority of internet traffic including web pages, email, and file transfers. Its reliability guarantees are what make the unreliable internet feel dependable to applications.
takeaways: TCP uses a three-way handshake to establish connections
Sequence numbers and acknowledgments ensure every byte arrives
Flow control and congestion control prevent network overload

faq.question: How does TCP handle lost packets?
faq.answer: TCP assigns sequence numbers to every byte and requires acknowledgment from the receiver. If an acknowledgment does not arrive within a timeout period, the sender retransmits the data. Fast retransmit triggers resending after three duplicate acknowledgments without waiting for the timeout.

faq.question: What is the TCP three-way handshake?
faq.answer: The client sends a SYN packet, the server responds with SYN-ACK, and the client replies with ACK. This three-step process establishes sequence numbers for both directions and confirms both sides are ready to communicate. It adds one round-trip of latency before data transfer begins.
